publication: New Jersey Herald News (combined with The Newark Herald)
summary: 12-page weekly, 15th Yr. No. 26, self-described 'New Jersey's oldest and only colored weekly of 12 pages or more,' published from 130 W. Kinney St., Newark. Front page leads with a conscientious objector (Bill Sutherland) resisting the draft, William R. Jackson named to Newark Board of Education, Baxter Terrace public housing tenant organizing, and the death sentence of Odell Waller in Virginia. Interior pages cover Senate politics (Lorenzo Harris vs. Sen. William Smathers), Elks and Masonic conventions, an all-Negro Coast Guard station at Pea Island NC, extensive society/wedding pages, an editorial page under publishers Frederick W. Martin and Richard L. Martin, community correspondent columns from a dozen NJ towns, an amusements/nightlife page, a sports page (Newark Eagles Negro National League, AAU track), and church news including Dorie Miller's Navy Cross ceremony photo.

incidents.what: Bill Sutherland Jr. of Glen Ridge, a conscientious objector, arrested/held by FBI in Hackensack for failing to report to CCC camp at Coshocton, Ohio; released on $500 bail
William R. Jackson named to Newark Board of Education by Mayor Vincent Murphy, first Black appointee in city's 106-year Board history alongside Joseph Kramer and Charles J. Fox
Odell Waller scheduled to die Thursday in Virginia electric chair unless Gov. Darden intervenes; case tied to poll-tax jury controversy
Admiral Nimitz pinned the Navy Cross on Dorie Miller aboard warship at Pearl Harbor for heroism during the Dec. 7, 1941 attack
All-white Grand Jury indictment of a Black man (Harraway) challenged as unconstitutional by NAACP counsel; case appealed to State Supreme Court

connections: Masthead states paper is 'combined with The Newark Herald,' confirming direct lineage/merger between the two mastheads being read in this batch
Coverage of Newark Eagles and Baltimore Elite Giants (Negro National League) ties to Black baseball history network
References to NAACP Newark branch membership drive (1,535 members) and NAACP national fair employment activism
